# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-25 (Extended v177)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to spring Year 7. Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house), Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire No. 6 (Gillenormand residence), Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Marché Saint-Jean, Rue des Billettes, Rue Saint-Denis, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, Rue Mondétour, Pointe Saint-Eustache, Rue du Cygne, Rue des Prêcheurs, Rue Blomet, Rue de Rivoli, Place Louis XV, Champs-Élysées, Esplanade, bridge of the Invalides, Hôtel des Princes, Hôtel Meurice, Rue Saint-Honoré, Passage Delorme, Place du Palais-Royal, Rue de Béthisy, Rue des Bourdonnais, Rue de la Poterie, Rue du Contrat-Social, Marché-aux-Poirées, Rue de Babylone, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Rue du Chaume, Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes, Royal Printing Establishment, river crossing at Dungate/Kelmere, harbor town of Wilholt/Elmhaven. English provincial towns: Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Kelford, Pontoise, Dungate, Torton, Quenford.

**Rumored claims (unverified)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately (winter Year 5). Fenelle Lindmere and Marald confided/revealed Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood (autumn Year 6).

**Established facts**: Kassa Brackick and Volan Stenworth married at Staveford; Kassa later went to Dungate. Taric Corrley quit Staveford, took lodgings in Dungate. Marald Corrford quit Dunstead, took lodgings in Salcombe; Fenelle Lindmere followed within month. Ismira Stenson quit Dungate, took lodgings in Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Matho Stenson went to Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Elra Corrford settled in Elmhaven. Havie Prydenridge promised Gadrek Prydenridge to pay old debt to Stenworth family (evening 24th June). Thizek Stenenridge told Elra Corrford deed to Kelmere pastures was forged (evening 24th June). Vesmira and Isvie bought and regretted ribbon purchases (evening 24th June). Kassa Stenson's husband gave solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Elra Corrford gave Matho Stenson solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven. New births and marriages: Rinelle Corrley and Kadrek Brackick had son Movus Brackick (Wilholt); Nerine Prydenridge and Lurald Stenworth wed at Ostcombe with half parish present, lived in Ostcombe thereafter.

**Spring Year 7 observations**: Isvie walked long way to avoid muddy square. Bremira Corrford and Isvie discussed weather, harvest, lame horse. Thizek walked long way to avoid muddy square. Taric Corrley remarked river was up at Dungate crossing; Kassa Stenson said it always was in spring. Taric Corrley bought ribbon, regretted it. Road rutted and puddled after thaw. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Rinelle hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Zavus Prydenridge hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Movie Prydenridge walked long way to avoid muddy square. Islan Thornmere and Nerine read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Cart with turnips passed well in Ostcombe. Ismira Stenson argued with carter over price of sack of oats (Elmhaven). Elra laughed at story nobody else found funny. Kadan hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step (Kelmere river crossing). Kadan Corrley and Rovus Prydenridge talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Matho counted coins twice, came up penny short (Elmhaven).

## Jean Valjean's Crisis and Discovery (Night of 24th June 1832, continuing into Spring Year 7)
**Blotting-book discovery**: Upon arriving at Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings, Valjean found Cosette's blotting-book open on sideboard before mirror. Mirror reflection revealed four lines—letter Cosette had written to young workman in Rue Plumet. **Valjean's collapse**: Understood Cosette was escaping; another was goal of her heart; he was no longer anything but her father. Soul gave utter roar. **Nature of his paternal love**: Into paternity his life's widowhood introduced all shades of love—daughter, mother, sister, woman, wife. Sentiment impossible to lose—pure with blindness's purity, celestial, angelic, divine. Destinies wedded though no marriage possible. **Spiritual crisis**: Grief surpassed bounds; quiver of revolt ran head to foot; immense reawakening of egotism; the *I* howled. Profound elements crumbling—fatal crisis. **Divination**: Recognized precipice—but was at bottom. Found man instantly: unknown prowler of Luxembourg, seeker of love adventures, coward making eyes at young girl with devoted father.

**During Spring Year 7**: Groped up stairs, hand trembling greatly; thought his actions smacked of theft. Unfolded Marius's note announcing death and love. In violent emotions, seized essential points. **Transformation**: Beheld splendor of death of hated individual, remained crushed with intoxicated amazement. **Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings**: Two sleeping-rooms, dining-room, kitchen, garret for Toussaint on second floor, back court. Initially slept well; awoke almost gay; recovered serenity and security. Twice or thrice Toussaint stammered about fighting in Paris—he paid no heed, absorbed in calculations.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (Autumn Year 5 through Evening 24th June 1832)
**Recognition and love**: Cosette acknowledged she never forgot Marius, always loved him. Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening, forcing old gate. At height of love's voluptuousness, remained absolutely chaste. **Confessions (spring Year 6, during cholera)**: Marius told Cosette—orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, father colonel and hero on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. Cosette told Marius—brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave to poor. **Éponine's death (evening 24th June)**: Éponine revealed she led Marius to barricade, spoke of her death as blessing, protected him from gunfire. Gave Marius letter from Cosette before dying. **Cosette's letter content**: Marriage impossible; grandfather refuses; no fortune either; hastened to him, he gone; kept promise given; dies; loves him. **Marius's response**: Covered letter with kisses; reflected Cosette going to England, nothing changed. Resolved to inform Cosette of death, send farewell, save Gavroche.

**Marius joins barricade (evening 24th June)**: Upon learning Valjean plans England departure in one week, arranged meeting 26th June at nine o'clock. Same evening, displaced bar at grating, rushed in. Cosette absent. Seated self with resolution, blessed love, said all left was to die. Mad with grief, one desire: speedy end. Voice summoned him to barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie. **Philosophy of duty**: Reflected on Colonel Pontmercy—proud soldier, guarded frontier, touched Asia, beheld cities, left blood, returned after twenty years scarred but pure. Own day come; must follow father, show bravery, seek death. Carries loaded pistols. **During first phase**: Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed; flung self into conflict. Saved Gavroche with first shot, delivered Courfeyrac with second. Seized powder barrel, glided along barricade to cage of paving-stones with torch, tore torch, replaced with powder barrel, stood foot on stones with torch in hand, dropped flame with startling cry. **Mental state**: Had furnace in brain; whirlwind outside himself. Two luminous months ending at frightful precipice, Cosette lost, barricade, M. Mabeuf killed, self leader—tremendous nightmare. Did not recognize Javert bound to post.

## Barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie (Evening 24th June 1832, into morning 6th June)
**Café Corinthe**: Ground floor with bar; first floor with billiard-table and wooden spiral staircase; cellar via trap-door; lodgings and attics. Proprietor: Widow Hucheloup. Serving-maids: Matelote, Gibelotte. **Two barricades**: Larger shut off Rue de la Chanvrerie; other closed Rue Mondétour. Interior: irregular square, twenty paces between grand barrier and lofty houses. Issue left free on Rue Mondétour opening to Halles. **Larger barricade (evening 24th June)**: Height six or seven feet, stepped construction, paling-stones, casks, wheels, omnibus pole with ropes, red flag. Forty-three insurgents commanded by Enjolras, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, etc. Six commanded by Feuilly at windows with guns.

**Javert's arrest**: Identified as Inspector of Police, aged fifty-two. Card, watch, purse with gold, sealed envelope with five lines in Prefect's handwriting discovered.

**Le Cabuc execution**: Enjolras executed him for killing, justified by insurrection needing discipline. Tradition: Le Cabuc was Claquesous.

**M. Mabeuf's sacrifice**: Venerable, austere, sold unique Diogenes Laertius, returned with hundred francs. Evening 24th June: followed band, refused arms. During attack: at detonation, tore flag from Enjolras. Eighty years old, white locks, aged arm upholding red banner. Enjolras eulogized: magnificent death; presence renders barricade impregnable.

**Unknown young figure**: Pale, thin, small, freckled, youthful artisan in tattered blouse and patched velvet trousers; spoke to Courfeyrac in peculiar voice. During attack: hand laid on muzzle when soldier aimed at Marius, shot traversed hand, artisan possibly struck and fell, but ball did not hit Marius.

**After first assault and repairs (into 6th June)**: Insurgents rallied, majority ascended to first-story window, commanded assailants. Medical students cared for wounded. Five gravely wounded men on mattresses in kitchen converted to ambulance; two municipal guardsmen attended first. Barricade repaired and augmented, raised two feet. Bars of iron planted resembled lances in rest. All sorts of rubbish added complicated external confusion. Redoubt cleverly made over into wall on inside, thicket on outside. Kitchen appropriated for ambulance, powder scattered on ground, bullets run, cartridges manufactured, lint scraped, fallen weapons redistributed, corpses removed.

**Provisions and morale (6th June, dawn)**: No repast possible. Neither bread nor meat. Fifty men exhausted scanty provisions during sixteen hours. Reached first hours of Spartan day when they would face inevitable attack. **Wine cache**: Fifteen full bottles hermetically sealed found in cellar. Enjolras placed veto on them, had bottles placed under table on which Father Mabeuf was lying to prevent Grantaire from drinking. **Unknown messenger**: Some unknown blouse-wearer appeared, stranger and passing hero, announced with inexorable resolution: whole army of Paris striking, third of army bearing down, National Guard advancing, shakos of fifth line and standards of sixth legion visible, attack in one hour, no populace stirring, nothing to expect, abandoned. Never known name of this man who vanished into shadows. **Insurgent resolve**: This resolution impregnated air of 6th June; on barricade Saint-Merry, insurgents raised clamor: "What matters it whether they come? Let us get ourselves killed, to the very last man." Insurgents full of hope, smiled waiting for dawn attack, no doubt as to success or cause, reckoned succor on way, divided day into three phases: six o'clock—regiment would turn; noon—insurrection of all Paris; sunset—revolution.

**Marius at dawn (6th June)**: Fasting, fevered, emerged from all hope, stranded in grief, saturated with violent emotions, conscious end was near, plunged into visionary stupor preceding fatal hour voluntarily accepted. Growing symptoms of febrile absorption known to science, suffering's voluptuousness. Despair's ecstasy. Looked on at everything as from without; things seemed far away; beheld men as through flame; heard voices as at bottom of abyss.

## Historical Note on June 1848 and the Barricade of Faubourg du Temple (Chapter 25)
Two most memorable barricades belong to fatal insurrection June 1848. Philosophy: exasperations of crowd which suffers and bleeds, violences contrary to principles which is its life, are popular coups d'état and should be repressed. Man of probity sacrifices himself, combats crowd out of love for it. Exasperations of people against itself. Attacked in name of revolution the revolution itself. Barricade faced Constituent Assembly, sovereignty of people, universal suffrage, nation, republic. Faubourg and redoubt lent each other assistance. Vast barricade spread like cliff against which strategy dashed itself. Mitraille vanished in shapelessness; bombs plunged into it; only holes from bullets. **Barricade of Faubourg du Temple**: Defended by eighty men, attacked by ten thousand, held out three days. On fourth, pierced houses, came over roofs, barricade taken. All killed except leader Barthélemy. Cournet: man of lofty stature, broad shoulders, red face, crushing fist, bold heart, loyal soul, sincere and terrible eye. Intrepid, energetic, irascible, stormy; most cordial of men, most formidable of combatants. Former naval officer. Something of Danton in Cournet; something of Hercules in Danton. **Later fatal circumstance**: In London, proscribed, Barthélemy slew Cournet in funereal duel. Caught in mysterious adventures, catastrophe where French justice sees extenuating circumstances, English justice only death. Barthélemy hanged. Unhappy being with possibly great intelligence, began in France with galleys, ended in England with gallows.

**Sixteen years context**: Sixteen years count in subterranean education of insurrection; June 1848 knew much more than June 1832. Barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie only outline and embryo compared to colossal barricades; formidable for that epoch.

## Philosophical Discussions (6th June, barricade)
Combeferre quoted and discussed classical figures—Harmodius and Aristogiton, Brutus, Chereas, Stephanus, Cromwell, Charlotte Corday, Sand—noting their moments of agony and remorse at striking men even for liberation. Compared translators of Georgics—Raux, Cournand, Delille, Malfilâtre—particularly prodigies of Cæsar's death. Discussion reverted to Brutus through mention of Cæsar. Combeferre argued Cæsar fell justly; severity toward Cæsar not diatribe but just arbitration in thought as Brutus's arbiter by sword. Noted Cæsar violated Rubicon, conferred dignities as though from himself, not rising at senate entrance, committed acts of king and tyrant. His twenty-three wounds touch less than spitting in face of Jesus Christ. Cæsar stabbed by senators; Christ cuffed by lackeys. One feels God through greater outrage.
